lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on financial crises, and Amit Varma’s dissent
lead.head: When bad gets worse, then worse
body: Every once in a while, Amit Varma said, the world seems to be falling apart: a financial crisis, inflation, bailouts. Ajay Shah, who has spent thirty years in the field as a participant, set out to explain why.
He began with a definition. Finance, Shah said, is the brain of the economy: it makes prices, allocates resources and solves people’s financing problems.

“A financial crisis is when there is a sudden and nonlinear impairment of the functions of finance,” he said. One firm failing is not a crisis, nor even a whole industry, if the work can be done another way. {119-C01}
The stakes are enormous, Shah argued. Financial crises are “upstream of wars and revolutions”, and he drew a direct line from the Great Depression to Adolf Hitler and the Second World War.
Nobody is a bystander. “You may not be interested in finance, but the financial system is interested in you,” he said. {119-C02}
## Stories first

All economics is rooted in economic history, Shah said, so he started with stories: New York in 1929, India in 1991, Harshad Mehta, the East Asian crisis, UTI in 2000, 2008 and the IL&FS default of 2018.

In each he hunted for the amplifier. A crash on one exchange is too small to shake the world, he said; it takes feedback loops, where “if things are bad, they get worse, and because they’re worse, they get worse.” {119-C03}
He was candid about his own record. Raj Chitale had warned him that UTI’s US-64 scheme would blow up, and he had not understood how broken it was. “I’m pointing a finger at me,” he said.
The response to 2008, run by Ben Bernanke and others schooled in the lessons of 1929, he held up as a model: let firms fail, but protect the functions of finance, whatever it takes.
## Why it keeps happening
From history Shah built a taxonomy of five types: banking, currency, debt, securities market and mixed crises. Each runs to a script. “I see financial crisis the way a doctor sees a cancer,” he said.

Crises will never end, he argued, for four reasons: human cognition, human cleverness, state failure and the fallacy of composition. Regulators will always be outwitted by the cleverest people in finance. {119-C12}
So the state should prepare rather than pretend. Shah’s toolkit runs from sound regulation of each firm to a lender of last resort, a law for resolving failed firms and a standing army of experts.
He rejected three extremes: pure laissez-faire, the populist story that bailouts protect fat cats, and the Indian reflex to “ban it”.
## The dissent
Varma had promised to keep his disagreements for the end, and he did. He has “great sympathy for the Austrian view”: that crises are caused by easy money, and made worse by the state.
“When I think about 2008, to me it was a failure of the state,” he said. {119-C16}
The argument that bailouts later made money did not move him: the cost, he said, falls on everyone’s taxes, the poorest included. Suppressing small failures, he warned, stores up bigger ones.

Both men ended on common ground. Ordinary citizens have skin in the game, Varma said, and should learn the basics. Shah agreed: nobody should treat financial crisis as “some exotic, far away subject”.

second.label: Learning from 1929
second.head: Sorry, Milton, we did it
second.deck: Ben Bernanke’s apology to Milton Friedman, and how it shaped 2008
body: In a 2002 speech, Ben Bernanke, then on the Federal Reserve’s board of governors but not yet its chairman, turned to Milton Friedman, who was on the stage with him. About the Great Depression, Bernanke said, the Fed had done it. {119-S07}
Ajay Shah called the moment doubly lovely. Bernanke gave Friedman the credit, but the two of them, with Anna Schwartz, had built the body of knowledge on what went wrong in 1929.

Six years later Bernanke chaired the Fed through the 2008 crisis and let its balance sheet grow roughly five-fold. {119-S08} “This is how great countries are made,” Shah said. Amit Varma called it a rare case of a thinker becoming a doer.

quote.text: Regarding the Great Depression, you’re right. We did it. We’re very sorry. But thanks to you, we won’t do it again.

second.caption: the Fed’s apology to Friedman

third.head: Fat cats, thin losses
body: The populist story of 2008, Ajay Shah said, is that taxpayers paid for the fat cats’ Lamborghinis. The data, he argued, say otherwise.

In the US, the Treasury put about $0.45 trillion into TARP, headed by Neel Kashkari. After the assets were sold, a GAO report put the loss at $31 billion, while the Fed’s crisis purchases were wildly profitable. {#tarp31} Taken together, the intervention made money.

He made the same point about UTI, with a confession. He had argued over its rescue with M. Damodaran, then heading UTI. The shares the government took were sold five years later at a big profit. “Damodaran was right, I was wrong.” {119-S10}
Amit Varma was unmoved. Who pays matters, he said, whatever the totals: bailouts are funded by everyone’s taxes, including those of the poorest. {119-C17}

p2.title: Anatomy of a crisis
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s helicopter tour of financial crises, from history to remedy, and the dissent of Amit Varma

sections.label: The definition
sections.head: The brain of the economy
sections.caption: what a financial crisis is
body: Finance, Ajay Shah said, is the brain of the economy. It decides who gets money, which industries and which technologies; it makes the prices that tell entrepreneurs where to invest; and it solves people’s problems of moving money across time, managing risk and funding large, complex projects.
A financial crisis, by his definition, is a sudden and nonlinear impairment of those functions. {119-C01}

The definition does a lot of work. One firm failing is not a crisis. Even a whole industry can collapse without one, if the economy can route the work through other channels. The point, Shah said, is to get things done. “We have no loyalty to finance as a means. We have a loyalty to the ends.”
## The attention span

We notice civil aviation, Shah said, only when an Air India plane crashes into a medical college hostel in Amdavad. Financial crises get the same short attention, though the world has been shaped by them. {119-J12}
Yet as individuals, he said, we all have skin in the game: when the financial system glitches, it imposes costs on firms and people all over the landscape. {119-C02}
~ Amit Varma, who calls himself a gentle listener in these conversations, promised to save his disagreements for a final chapter. He kept the promise.

quote.text: A financial crisis is when there is a sudden and nonlinear impairment of the functions of finance.

sections.label: The playbook
sections.head: Lend freely, and make them cry
sections.caption: the Friedman-Bernanke playbook
body: Is there a case for the state? First ask whether there is a market failure, Ajay Shah said, and here there is: a negative externality. A small firm like Swapnalok Studios, heading for an IPO, can be hurt by a crisis for no fault of its own. Amit Varma cautioned that the state need not act on every externality.
Shah then set out the reading of the Great Depression built by Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz and a young Ben Bernanke. The Fed, in their view, made three mistakes.

First, it failed as lender of last resort. Walter Bagehot’s rule, in Shah’s words, is to lend freely against good collateral at a penal rate: “So people should cry when they come asking for credit from a central bank.” {119-J13}
Second, it let the money supply contract, and the deflation that followed raised the real burden of every debt. Third, as banks died, what they knew about their borrowers died too.
## Functions, not firms
The remedy is to let firms fail but protect the functions. “We have no loyalty to banks, we have no loyalty to NBFCs,” Shah said. {119-C09}
~ In 2008 the Fed did just that. It let Bear Stearns and Lehman go, grew its balance sheet from about $0.9 trillion to $4.5 trillion, and kept inflation under control. {119-S08}

quote.text: It takes a thinker to say we will do what it takes. And if it takes five X, we’ll do five X.

sections.label: The five types
sections.head: Every crisis has a script
sections.caption: the five types of crisis
body: Around the world, Ajay Shah said, there are about five financial crises a year in one country or another. {#fiveayear} He sorts them into five types.

Banking crises come first. Shah borrowed Merton Miller’s description of banking as a disaster-prone nineteenth-century industry. Indian banks run about 20 times leverage, so a five per cent loss wipes them out, and their loans are opaque and illiquid. {119-C08}
Banks also attract political looting, for the reason the bank robber gave: “because that’s where the money is.” {119-J10}

Currency crises are macroeconomics. Debt crises turn on whether the interest rate outruns the growth of the top line. India masks the problem by forcing the financial system to lend cheaply to the government. “We basically violate the Magna Carta,” Shah said. {119-J17}
## The inner sanctum

Securities markets, he said, are “the commanding heights of the financial system”. In an illiquid market like India’s corporate bonds, one large sale can set off falling prices, falling NAVs and more redemptions. {119-C11}
The cure is a deep, liquid market open to everyone: “there should be algorithmic traders, there should be astrology traders.”
~ The fifth type mixes the others, as in Indonesia. Anyone who has not lived through a crisis, Shah said, should learn the scripts from books.

quote.text: Banks are a disaster prone 19th century industry. And they will go wrong because you have too much leverage.

sections.label: The causes
sections.head: Spy versus spy, forever
sections.caption: why crises keep happening
body: Ajay Shah offered no grand unified theory of why crises happen, but four elements of one.

The first is human cognition. Someone who spends twenty good years in a boom forgets that things can go wrong, and the trader with the biggest leverage looks like a hero. Statisticians who fit models on the last five or ten good years make the same error.
“Those who fail to learn from history are doomed to participate in its repetition,” he said. {119-J11}
## Cat and mouse
The second is cleverness. Regulators and bankers play a cat-and-mouse game, Shah said, like *Spy versus Spy* in *Mad Magazine*. {119-J09} “Are you thirteen again?” Amit Varma asked.
Bankers with lopsided payoffs find the chinks in every rule, and some of the smartest people in the world work in finance. Regulation will always play catch-up. {119-C12}

The third is state failure: public choice problems and regulators with too much power. The fourth is the fallacy of composition: making each bank safe does not make the system safe, because many moves in one direction add up to an avalanche.
~ To believe that brilliant regulators could end crises, Shah said, is an illusion of control. Whatever we build will foul up, over and over.

quote.text: The brain power of Goldman Sachs will always exceed the brain power of the regulators.

sections.label: The remedies
sections.head: A standing army for bad days
sections.caption: the crisis toolkit
body: What can be done? Ajay Shah’s first step is microprudential regulation: getting each firm right, one at a time. It is not enough, he said, but it is necessary, and India has a long history of failing at it.
Second, a lender of last resort. “We in India have not begun,” he said.

Third, a resolution framework, so that financial firms can go bankrupt while small savers, the grandmothers and dentists, are protected. The Financial Resolution Bill that came out of FSLRC ran into opposition from bank unions and stalled.
## The ninjas

Fourth, and messiest, a standing army: experts, data and authority, perhaps in the Department of Economic Affairs, for the crises nobody designed for. Shah pointed to the Office of Financial Research that America built after 2008. {119-C13}
He ended with a heresy. A good banking system is “a first world thing”, he said, and India is at best 25 years from one; until then, banks should stay small. {119-C14}
~ “I hate to pick winners, I hate to pick losers. But I am proposing a loser,” Shah said. Amit Varma was wary: “Don’t use state coercion to get there.” {119-J07}

quote.text: And so we need an unpredictable team of ninjas which will be able to deal with these things as they come along.

sections.label: The dissent
sections.head: Let the small fires burn
sections.caption: the Austrian view
body: Amit Varma saved his disagreement for the last chapter. He has great sympathy, he said, for the Austrian view: that crises begin with easy money from central banks and are deepened by the state.

The roaring twenties ran on easy credit from the Fed, he said, and the years before 2008 on Alan Greenspan’s cheap money. After 1929, he said, citing Thomas Sowell, the economy began recovering within months, until government intervention made it worse. {119-R16}
He disputed Ajay Shah’s view that Hitler’s spending revived Germany: the German economy, Varma said, was coming back to speed by 1923, before Hitler came to power. {#germany}
On 2008 he cited the Community Reinvestment Act, Fannie and Freddie and the rating agencies. It was a failure of the state, he said, not of capitalism. {119-C16}
## Let it flood
Bailouts create moral hazard, privatising profits and socialising losses. That they made money years later, Varma argued, does not wash: the cost falls on everyone’s taxes, the poorest included.

From James C. Scott’s *In Praise of Floods* he drew a parable. Embankments raise a river above the land until the flood is far worse; putting out every small forest fire builds fuel for one the size of a state. {119-C18}
~ Be sceptical of convention, he concluded, not dismissive of it, and keep reading economic history. {119-C19}

quote.text: The taxes of the beggar at the traffic signal who pays a GST when she buys salt and soap.

side.boxText: Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz and a young Ben Bernanke worked out what went wrong in 1929. Ajay Shah’s summary of their lessons: act as lender of last resort, never let money contract, and protect the functions of finance. {119-C09}

contQuote.text: The market economy is not a tidy, centrally planned company town. The market economy is an unpredictable bubbling of the human heart, figuring out new things all the time.

p3.title: Crash course
p3.deck: Four stories from the history of crises, and what each teaches

stories.start: The uh starting point I want to take is the United States stock market
stories.end: So it was not a great success in terms of an intellectual edifice.
stories.caption: the crash of 1929
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the crash that brought down the whole world
stories.head: New York falls, the world follows
body: Ajay Shah did not claim that financial crises began in 1929: there had been tulip mania, paper money gone bad and banking crises long before. But 1929, he said, is a lovely place to start.
Through the roaring twenties, as they are called, the American and global economy already had difficulties, and the Fed, the world’s most important central bank, had not been doing a great job.
Then, for reasons still not deeply understood today, the New York Stock Exchange crashed in 1929. {119-S01}

A fall in share prices on one exchange is not big enough to shake the world, Shah said. What did it was a chain: the crash triggered something, which triggered something else. Bank failures made the economy worse, and a worse economy felled more banks. {119-C03}
At the peak, something like 30 per cent of the American banking system went bankrupt. {#thirty} Within months, the crash was showing up in India. {#india1929}
The gravest consequence was in Germany. “There is a direct line between the Great Depression and Adolf Hitler,” Shah said. That, he argued, is why the fate of the world is on the line.

~ There was a twist in the recovery. Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Hitler, Shah said, ran policies that would now be called Keynesian without Keynes’s ideas. They improvised, “through seat of the pants”. Keynes’s ideas, he added, have had a middling record when applied to later depressions.
stories.why: A crash in one market cannot shake the world on its own; it needs amplifiers. To understand any crisis, Shah said, look for the feedback loop that makes bad worse. {119-C03}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma later disputed that Hitler’s spending revived Germany: its economy, he said, was coming back to speed by 1923, before Hitler took power. {#germany}

stories.start: I want to talk about the Indian balance of payments crisis of 1991.
stories.end: And that was the Indian balance of payments crisis.
stories.caption: the rupee crisis of 1991
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s balance of payments crisis of 1991
stories.head: A run through narrow lanes
body: A country imports the gap between what it invests and what it saves, Ajay Shah said. {119-C04} Through the late 1980s, India’s fiscal deficits grew, worst of all in the political instability after Rajiv Gandhi, eating into savings and raising the need for foreign capital.
Then Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait, and remittances took a hit. Capital controls meant money could enter only through a few *patli gallis*, narrow lanes, and these choked. {119-S02}

Once everyone was sure the rupee would crash, everyone bet on it. Exporters kept their dollars abroad, importers bought dollars early, and Indians moved assets out, waiting to bring the money back after the fall.
~ The lesson, for Shah, is resilience: India needs twenty big channels for capital, with no involvement of the government. {119-C05}

quote.text: Once everybody believes that the rupee has to depreciate greatly, then every thinking person is trying to bet on that

stories.start: And the greatest hero of this is George Soros, who look thought deeply
stories.end: no government can stand up to the combined power of the global financial system
stories.caption: George Soros and the pound
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on George Soros and the Bank of England
stories.head: The day the pound broke
body: George Soros, Ajay Shah said, is the greatest hero of the currency crisis. He thought deeply about the dilemma facing the Bank of England.

Keeping the pound in the European exchange rate mechanism would need a sharp rise in interest rates. The economy was already weak and elections were near. Why, Soros reckoned, would a government kick its own economy in the face?
So he bet the pound would break out, and in one day made a profit of over a billion dollars. {#billion}

~ Once a few traders bet against a currency, hundreds more join, because their bets can make the collapse happen; Amit Varma noted that Soros called this reflexivity. “No government can stand up to the combined power of the global financial system,” Shah said. {119-S05}
stories.why: A currency crisis is macroeconomics, Shah said. Whoever understands the trade-off a government faces between its peg and its economy can tell whether the peg will hold, and markets punish the policy that cannot. {119-C07}

stories.start: Bananke tells a story around the role that banks played in that United States.
stories.end: So this was the critical insight of Bern K.
stories.caption: the friendly neighbourhood banker
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah retells Ben Bernanke’s insight on lost knowledge
stories.head: What the bank manager knew
body: Picture a bank in pre-digital America, Ajay Shah said. No computers, no models, just branches, loan officers and paper files. The manager lives among his borrowers and knows whether they are upstanding members of the community.
Shah cast himself as the borrower, a man so temperate that “I only have milk in a bar.” The manager knows that, and knows his repayment history. {119-J02}

Then the bank fails, for no fault of either, because it lent against shares in New York. Shah goes to the next bank, run by Vaishnav, who has no history with him: “Let’s get started with a 10 rupee loan.” {119-S09}
~ Multiply that across 30 per cent of America’s banks, he said, and coffee shops and small manufacturers everywhere are choked of working capital just when they need it.

quote.text: This history is in your skull. And this history is in your files.

quiz.q: What did Ben Bernanke tell Milton Friedman, on stage in 2002, about the Great Depression?
quiz.a: That the Fed did it, was very sorry, and would not do it again.

quiz.q: What was Walter Bagehot’s rule for a lender of last resort, in Shah’s words?
quiz.a: Lend freely against good collateral at a penal rate, so borrowers cry.

quiz.q: What emerged about Thailand’s central bank on the day “all hell broke loose”?
quiz.a: Its secret forward sales of the baht exceeded its entire reserves.

quiz.q: How did Yashwant Sinha split the cost of rescuing the unit holders of US-64?
quiz.a: Fifty-fifty: public money paid half, and unit holders bore the other half.

quiz.q: Which book did Amit Varma cite for small floods and fires preventing big ones?
quiz.a: James C. Scott’s *In Praise of Floods*, applied to bailouts and moral hazard.
